paras.en: [[9:20|He that feared the word of the Lord among Pharao's servants|Qui timuit verbum Domini de servis Pharaonis]], [[9:20|made his servants and his cattle flee into houses|fecit confugere servos suos et jumenta in domos]], that is, the servants of Pharao and the other Egyptians whom God's threat, made through Moses, reached, and who believed it and feared with servile fear and dread that it would be fulfilled, did not let their servants and cattle be in the fields. [[9:21|But he that regarded not the word of the Lord|Qui autem neglexit sermonem Domini]], that is, despised the words of God spoken through Moses and did not believe them, [[9:21|left his servants, and his cattle in the fields|dimisit servos suos et jumenta in agris]]. For at times servants and certain cattle stayed day and night in the plains and pastures, at the season suited to it.

paras.t: Et dixit Dominus ad Moysen: Extende manum tuam in cœlum, ut fiat grando in universa terra Ægypti, etc. Extenditque Moyses virgam in cœlum aereum, erigendo manum cum virga versus cœlum; et Dominus dedit tonitrua et grandinem, ac discurrentia fulgura super terram. Quæ tria supernaturaliter generabantur in aere. Sicque plaga ista continuit in se plures plagas particulares, et fuit terribilis nimis, imo tanto terribilior, quanto inconsuetior in Ægypto. Tonitrua quoque afflixerunt ac terruerunt auditum, fulgura visum; grandines tactum, sed et visum atque auditum.
paras.en: [[9:22|And the Lord said to Moses: Stretch forth thy hand towards heaven|Et dixit Dominus ad Moysen: Extende manum tuam in cœlum]], [[9:22|that there may be hail in the whole land of Egypt|ut fiat grando in universa terra Ægypti]], etc. [[9:23|And Moses stretched forth his rod towards heaven|Extenditque Moyses virgam in cœlum]], the heaven of the air, raising his hand with the rod towards the sky; [[9:23|and the Lord sent thunder and hail|et Dominus dedit tonitrua et grandinem]], [[9:23|and lightnings running along the ground|ac discurrentia fulgura super terram]]. These three were produced supernaturally in the air. And so this plague contained in itself several particular plagues, and was exceedingly terrible, nay, the more terrible the more unaccustomed it was in Egypt. The thunders afflicted and terrified the hearing, the lightnings the sight, the hail the touch, and the sight and hearing as well.

paras.t: Pluitque Dominus grandinem super terram Ægypti. Et grando et ignis, utpote fulgur assiduum valde terrificum, mixta pariter ferebantur: sicque plaga intolerabilior fuit. Et percussit grando cuncta quæ fuerunt in agris ab homine usque ad jumentum inclusive, quia tam homines quam jumenta in agris occidit. Cunctamque herbam agri percussit grando, gramina et terræ nascentia destruendo, et omne lignum regionis Ægypti confregit. Quidam scribit, quod dura videlicet ligna, non fuerunt fracta. Cujus oppositum dicit hæc littera, nisi forsan dicatur, quod arbores in superioribus suis partibus, quæ tenuiores sunt, fractæ fuerunt, non autem in stipite.
paras.en: [[9:23|and the Lord rained hail upon the land of Egypt|Pluitque Dominus grandinem super terram Ægypti]]. [[9:24|And the hail and fire|Et grando et ignis]], that is, lightning, unceasing and most terrifying, [[9:24|mixt with it drove on together|mixta pariter ferebantur]]: and so the plague was the more unbearable. [[9:25|And the hail destroyed|Et percussit grando]] [[9:25|all things that were in the fields|cuncta quæ fuerunt in agris]], [[9:25|both man and beast|ab homine usque ad jumentum]], inclusively, since it killed both men and beasts in the fields. [[9:25|and the hail smote every herb of the field|Cunctamque herbam agri percussit grando]], destroying the grass and all that grows from the earth, [[9:25|and it broke every tree of the country|et omne lignum regionis Ægypti confregit]] of Egypt. A certain writer says that the hard trees, that is, were not broken. The text here says the opposite, unless perhaps it be said that the trees were broken in their upper parts, which are slenderer, but not in the trunk.

paras.t: Misitque Pharao, et vocavit Moysen et Aaron, dicens: Peccavi etiam nunc. Orate Dominum ut desinant tonitrua Dei et grando: per quæ intellexit et fulgurum cessationem; ut dimittam vos, et nequaquam ultra hic maneatis. Hæc Pharaonis confessio non venit ex vera pœnitentia seu contritione, sed ex quadam coactione et servili timore.
paras.en: [[9:27|And Pharao sent and called Moses and Aaron, saying|Misitque Pharao, et vocavit Moysen et Aaron, dicens]]: [[9:27|I have sinned this time also|Peccavi etiam nunc]]. [[9:28|Pray ye to the Lord that the thunderings of God and the hail may cease|Orate Dominum ut desinant tonitrua Dei et grando]]: by which he meant the ceasing of the lightnings too; [[9:28|that I may let you go, and that ye may stay here no longer|ut dimittam vos, et nequaquam ultra hic maneatis]]. This confession of Pharao did not come from true penitence or contrition, but from a kind of compulsion and servile fear.

paras.t: Ait Moyses: Quum egressus fuero de urbe ista, in qua nunc tecum sum, extendam palmas meas ad Dominum, id est, mentem cum manibus elevabo ad Deum, ipsum rogando pro cessatione plagæ istius. Dicuntur autem manus levari ad Dominum, in quantum ex interna devotione extenduntur in cœlum, in quo Deus specialiter esse et habitare perhibetur, in quantum ibidem clarius se ostendit et evidentius operatur, quum tamen ipse proprie illocalis, intemporalisque sit, utpote simplicissimus et prorsus incircumscriptus. Et cessabunt tonitrua, et grando non erit, id est diutius non durabit; ut scias quia Domini est terra, id est, quod Deus noster jure creationis et gubernationis sit Dominus terræ, et omnium quæ in ea sunt, ita quod dii tui te et cultores suos ceteros nequeunt adjuvare. Pharao pluraliter dixit, Orate: sed Moyses tanquam principalis, singulariter respondit, Extendam, etc. Et quia hæc grando supernaturaliter producebatur divina virtute, cujus et ostensiva fuit, ideo recte vocavit eam Pharao grandinem Dei.
paras.en: [[9:29|Moses said: As soon as I am gone out of the city|Ait Moyses: Quum egressus fuero de urbe]], this city in which I now am with thee, [[9:29|I will stretch forth my hands to the Lord|extendam palmas meas ad Dominum]], that is, I will lift up my mind with my hands to God, asking him for the ceasing of this plague. Now the hands are said to be lifted up to the Lord inasmuch as, from inward devotion, they are stretched out towards heaven, where God is said in a special way to be and to dwell, inasmuch as there he shows himself more clearly and works more manifestly; though he himself is, properly speaking, in no place and in no time, being most simple and wholly uncircumscribed. [[9:29|and the thunders shall cease, and the hail shall be no more|Et cessabunt tonitrua, et grando non erit]], that is, will last no longer; [[9:29|that thou mayst know that the earth is the Lord's|ut scias quia Domini est terra]][[Ps 23:1||]], that is, that our God, by right of creation and government, is Lord of the earth and of all that is in it, so that thy gods cannot help thee or their other worshippers. Pharao said in the plural, [[9:28|Pray ye|Orate]]; but Moses, as the principal, answered in the singular, [[9:29|I will stretch forth|Extendam]], etc. And because this hail was produced supernaturally by divine power, and also showed that power, Pharao rightly called it the hail of God [in v. 28 the words are "the thunderings of God and the hail"].

paras.t: Præterea quæri potest, qualiter servi Pharaonis, durante hac plaga, poterant sine læsione ire ad Moysen. Ad quod quis dicere posset, quod omni qua poterant arte et munitione se texerant. Aut forte ideo plaga non tetigit eos, quia ad Moysen ibant pro misericordia impetranda.
paras.en: Further, it may be asked how Pharao's servants could go to Moses without harm while this plague lasted. To which one might say that they had covered themselves with every art and protection they could. Or perhaps the plague did not touch them because they were going to Moses to obtain mercy.

paras.t: Novi autem quod tu et servi tui necdum timeatis Dominum Deum filiali aut saltem initiali timore, sed solum servili: quod non est absolute et proprie Deum timere, sed aliqualiter tantum, quum scriptum sit: Qui timet Deum, nihil negligit. Et item: Beati omnes qui timent Dominum. Interdum tamen dicit Scriptura serviliter timentes timere Deum, ut dum quarto Regum de Samaritanis asseritur: Fuerunt igitur gentes istæ timentes quidem Dominum, et nihilo minus idolis suis servientes.
paras.en: [[9:30|But I know that neither thou, nor thy servants do yet fear the Lord God|Novi autem quod tu et servi tui necdum timeatis Dominum Deum]] with filial or at least initial fear, but only with servile fear [servile fear dreads punishment; filial fear dreads offending God, out of love; initial fear is the beginning of charity, partly the one and partly the other]: which is not to fear God simply and properly, but only in a manner, since it is written: [[Eccles 7:19|he that feareth God, neglecteth nothing|Qui timet Deum, nihil negligit]]. And again: [[Ps 127:1|Blessed are all they that fear the Lord|Beati omnes qui timent Dominum]]. Yet at times Scripture says that those who fear servilely fear God, as when it is said of the Samaritans in the fourth book of Kings: [[4 Kings 17:41|So these nations feared the Lord, but nevertheless served also their idols|Fuerunt igitur gentes istæ timentes quidem Dominum, et nihilo minus idolis suis servientes]].

paras.t: Linum ergo et hordeum læsum est, id est destructum grandine atque fulguribus: nempe quæ grandinis læsionem evaserant, fulgure cæsa sunt; eo quod hordeum esset virens, id est in tantum excreverat, quod rursus post læsionem non poterat fructuose renasci, seu crescere, et linum jam folliculos germinaret, id est, non poterat utiliter denuo crescere, quia folliculi erant corrupti. Triticum autem et far non sunt læsa, quia serotina erant, id est nondum viruerant, nec prodierant in spicam, quoniam tardius nascebantur; aut si parum excreverant, et extremitas læsa est, quod renascebatur validum fuit. Porro far est genus grani grossius frumento, ut Magister in historiis ait. Unde secundum Lyram, in Hebræo habetur, spelta. Potius tamen reor, quod nomen illud Hebræum ad utrumque æquivocum sit.
paras.en: [[9:31|The flax therefore, and the barley were hurt|Linum ergo et hordeum læsum est]], that is, destroyed by the hail and the lightnings: for what had escaped harm from the hail was struck down by the lightning; [[9:31|because the barley was green|eo quod hordeum esset virens]], that is, it had grown so far that after the harm it could not spring up again with fruit, or grow; [[9:31|and the flax was now bolled|et linum jam folliculos germinaret]], that is, it could not usefully grow again, since the bolls were spoiled. [[9:32|But the wheat, and other winter corn were not hurt|Triticum autem et far non sunt læsa]] [the Latin has far, which the Douay-Rheims renders "other winter corn"], [[9:32|because they were lateward|quia serotina erant]], that is, they had not yet grown green nor come into the ear, since they came up later; or if they had grown a little and the tips were harmed, what sprang up again was strong. Now far is a kind of grain coarser than wheat, as the Master says in the Histories [Peter Comestor, in the Historia scholastica]. Hence according to Lyra the Hebrew has "spelt". Yet I rather think that that Hebrew word is equivocal, covering both.

paras.t: Egressusque Moyses a Pharaone ex urbe, tetendit manus ad Dominum, orando devote in loco quieto et corde jam quietato, unde in tumultu Pharaonico noluit pro hac causa orare; et cessaverunt tonitrua et grando, et etiam fulgura, nec ultra stillavit pluvia super terram. Ex hoc elicitur, quod in hac plaga fuit etiam pluvia valde impetuosa, terræ nascentibus nociva, Ægyptiisque terrorem incutiens, quia in terra illa rarissime pluit; et pluvia ibidem est fecundationi terræ obstaculo, quia naturale est terræ illi ex Nili inundatione irrigari et fecundari. Solet autem pluvia tonitrua comitari, juxta illud: Fulgura in pluviam fecit, id est terminavit. […] hæc mala, […]. In quo admiranda obstinatio ejus patet.
paras.en: [[9:33|And when Moses was gone from Pharao out of the city, he stretched forth his hands to the Lord|Egressusque Moyses a Pharaone ex urbe, tetendit manus ad Dominum]], praying devoutly in a quiet place and with a heart now quieted; hence he would not pray for this cause amid Pharao's tumult; [[9:33|and the thunders and the hail ceased|et cessaverunt tonitrua et grando]], and the lightnings too, [[9:33|neither did there drop any more rain upon the earth|nec ultra stillavit pluvia super terram]]. From this it is gathered that in this plague there was also a very violent rain, harmful to what grows from the earth and striking terror into the Egyptians, because in that land it very seldom rains; and there rain is a hindrance to the fruitfulness of the land, since it is natural to that land to be watered and made fruitful by the flooding of the Nile. Now rain usually goes with thunder, according to the verse: [[Ps 134:7|he hath made lightnings for the rain|Fulgura in pluviam fecit]], that is, made them end in rain [the margin is partly lost and shows only "… 7"; the words are those of Ps 134:7, also found in Jer 51:16]. […] these evils, […]. In which his astonishing obstinacy is plain.

paras.t: Circa hæc quæritur, qualiter in hac plaga septima dicantur jumenta in agris occisa, quum tamen in isto capitulo dictum sit, quod in quinta plaga mortua sint omnia animantia Ægyptiorum. Respondetur, quod in quinta plaga occisa sunt jumenta quæ tunc erant in campis, sed in domibus multa manserunt, quæ vel omnia vel partim in septima plaga in agris perempta sunt. Denique in Scholastica historia tangitur, quod et credibile satis est, utpote quod plagæ istæ non contigerunt sine multo temporis intervallo, in quo poterant Ægyptii jumenta aliunde acquirere. Imo in glossa Scholasticæ historiæ fertur, quod forte per quinquennium, vel eo amplius duraverunt successive hæ plagæ. Verumtamen potius arbitror, quod infra unum annum fuerunt inductæ: fuerunt enim quodammodo continuatæ, prout ex textu videtur elici posse. Communiter enim, descripta cessatione plagarum, subjungitur: Et induratum est cor ejus et servorum illius Pharaonis, et non dimisit populum, sicut præceperat Dominus per manum Moysis. Per quod datur intelligi, quod licentiam quam ante cessationem plagarum dedit aut dare promisit, plagis sopitis, mox revocavit, aut prorsus petitionem negavit. Et sic post aliquantulum tempus Moyses suam legationem continuando, ex Dei imperio ad Pharaonem pro eadem redit causa, et aliam plagam prædixit, quæ et statim infligebatur.
paras.en: On this it is asked how in this seventh plague the cattle are said to have been killed in the fields, although it was said in this chapter that in the fifth plague all the beasts of the Egyptians died. The answer is that in the fifth plague the cattle that were then in the plains were killed, but many remained in the houses, and these, all or some of them, perished in the fields in the seventh plague. Then the Scholastic History touches on this, which is credible enough: that these plagues did not happen without a long interval of time, in which the Egyptians could get cattle from elsewhere. Indeed, the gloss on the Scholastic History says that these plagues lasted, one after another, perhaps for five years or more. Yet I rather judge that they were brought on within a single year: for they were in a manner continuous, as it seems can be gathered from the text. For commonly, once the ceasing of the plagues has been described, it is added: [[9:35|And his heart was hardened, and the heart of his servants|Et induratum est cor ejus et servorum illius]], that is, of Pharao, [[9:35|neither did he let the children of Israel go, as the Lord had commanded by the hand of Moses|et non dimisit populum, sicut præceperat Dominus per manum Moysis]] [Denis has "the people" where this verse has "the children of Israel"]. By this we are given to understand that the leave which he gave, or promised to give, before the plagues ceased, he soon revoked once they were stilled, or flatly refused the request. And so after a little time Moses, carrying on his embassy, returns at God's command to Pharao for the same cause, and foretells another plague, which also was inflicted at once.

paras.t: Postremo, hæc septima plaga fuit partim ex aqua, quia grando et pluvia erant in ea; partim ex igne, quia ignis et grando commixtim ferebantur in aere; partim quoque ex aere, propter tonitrua quæ erant soni in aere facti, cum ingenti collisione commotioneque aeris. Est quippe tonitruum, exstinctio ignis in nube, secundum Philosophum. Quod tamen per prædicationem causalem verificatur, quia ex ipsa exstinctione vaporis ignei in nube sonus producitur, qui est tonitruum. Fuerunt autem in plaga hac nubes copiosæ, ac de se supernaturaliter productæ in aere per ministeria angelorum. Correspondet quoque hæc plaga culpæ Ægyptiorum, qua Hebræos multipliciter afflixerunt in decoctione laterum per aquam et ignis incendium, et in collectionibus palearum per terram et aerem.
paras.en: Lastly, this seventh plague was partly of water, since hail and rain were in it; partly of fire, since fire and hail were borne along mingled together in the air; and partly of air, because of the thunders, which were sounds made in the air with a huge clashing and stirring of the air. For thunder, according to the Philosopher, is the quenching of fire in a cloud. This, however, is true by causal predication [that is, the thing is named by its cause: the quenching is not itself the sound but produces it], since from the very quenching of the fiery vapour in the cloud a sound is produced, which is thunder. And in this plague there were abundant clouds, and these too were produced supernaturally in the air through the ministry of angels. This plague also answers to the fault of the Egyptians, by which they afflicted the Hebrews in many ways: in the baking of bricks by water and the burning of fire, and in the gathering of straw over the land and in the air.

9.title: De spirituali ejusdem capituli noni intellectu
9.title_en: On the spiritual understanding of the same ninth chapter

paras.t: Per plagas in isto capitulo descriptas edocemur, quod Deus quantum in se est, multipliciter per prodigia ac flagella, per prospera et adversa, exhortatur et provocat homines etiam reprobos et perversos, ad vitam salubrem, et ad divinorum recognitionem beneficiorum ac mirabilium suorum effectuum. Et quo homines diutius obtemperare abnuerint, eo acrius flagellari merentur.
paras.en: By the plagues described in this chapter we are taught that God, as far as in Him lies, in many ways, by prodigies and scourges, by prosperity and adversity, exhorts and calls men, even the reprobate and perverse, to a wholesome life and to the acknowledgement of the divine benefits and of His wonderful works. And the longer men refuse to obey, the more sharply they deserve to be scourged.

paras.t: Porro per devastationem agrorum Ægyptiorum, spiritualiter denotatur, quod corda rebellium et pravorum, omni virtutum virore, omni gratiæ pulchritudine ob suas privantur perversitates, imo et in naturalibus vulnerantur atque fœdantur. Per interfectionem autem pecorum designatur, quod motus passionum et concupiscentiæ bestiales moriuntur in impiis: non quod in eis esse desistunt; sed dum per rationis censuram et per actiones virtutum non refrenantur, mortalia vitia fiunt. Sicque in se ipsis sunt mortui motus, quoniam vita gratiæ carent et sua occidunt subjecta, quemadmodum in Apocalypsi fertur ad quemdam: Nomen habes quod vivas, sed mortuus es. Præterea, Ægyptii merito in suorum interitu pecorum sunt puniti, quia et animalia miserrima coluerunt, atque in similitudinibus jumentorum suos venerati sunt deos, ut dictum est. Ideo per quæ peccaverunt, per ea puniti sunt.
paras.en: Further, by the laying waste of the fields of the Egyptians it is spiritually denoted that the hearts of the rebellious and wicked are, for their perversities, stripped of all the greenness of the virtues and of all the beauty of grace; nay, they are even wounded and defiled in their natural powers [an echo of the scholastic saying that by sin man is despoiled of the gifts of grace and wounded in what belongs to his nature]. And by the killing of the cattle it is signified that the motions of the passions and the bestial concupiscences die in the wicked: not that they cease to exist in them, but that, while they are not reined in by the judgement of reason and by acts of virtue, they become deadly vices. And so these motions are dead in themselves, since they lack the life of grace, and they slay the souls in which they are, as is said to a certain one in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 3:1|thou hast the name of being alive. And thou art dead|Nomen habes quod vivas, sed mortuus es]]. Moreover, the Egyptians were deservedly punished in the destruction of their cattle, because they also worshipped the most wretched animals, and venerated their gods in the likenesses of beasts[[Wis 12:24||]], as has been said. Therefore by the things through which they sinned, by the same they were punished[[Wis 12:23||]] [the margin gives Wis. xii, 23; Denis's words are closest to Wis 11:17, By what things a man sinneth, by the same also he is tormented].

paras.t: Per sextam vero plagam, puta per ulcera, vesicas turgentes, incensiones viscerum internorum et vulnera, designatur, quod dum iniqui emendari dedignantur per exterioris ablationem substantiæ, merentur in propriis personis atque corporibus tangi, lædi et cruciari. Per ulcera quoque specialiter significatur pravarum cogitationum collectio, ad impia facta inclinans, seque erigens, et per signa demonstrans. Ulcus namque causatur ex aggregatione humorum peccantium, ob quorum abundantiam gignitur tumor. Per vesicas turgentes, intelliguntur interiores indispositiones culpabiles ac pœnales, quæ ex gula, præsertim ex immoderantia potus, nascuntur; per vulnera aperta, opera vitiosa: per incensiones viscerum, inflammationes iræ, impatientiæ, indignationis. Omnibus vitiis istis permittit sanctus et justus Deus sauciari ac perire iniquos, quorum omnia interiora sunt inordinata, et sibimetipsis frequenter sunt graves: quia ut loquitur Isaias, Iniqui sunt quasi mare fervens, quod quiescere non potest.
paras.en: By the sixth plague, that is, by the boils, the swelling blains, the burnings of the inward parts and the wounds, it is signified that when the wicked disdain to be amended by the taking away of their outward substance, they deserve to be touched, hurt and tormented in their own persons and bodies. By the boils, too, is signified in particular the gathering together of wicked thoughts, which inclines to impious deeds, rises up, and shows itself by outward signs. For a boil is caused by a gathering of peccant humours [humores peccantes, literally "sinning humours": the physicians' term for humours in excess or corrupted], from whose abundance a swelling arises. By the swelling blains are understood inward disorders, both culpable and penal [that is, both sins and punishments of sin], which spring from gluttony, especially from immoderate drinking; by the open wounds, vicious works; by the burnings of the inward parts, the inflammations of anger, impatience and indignation. The holy and just God permits the wicked to be wounded and to perish by all these vices, for all that is within them is disordered, and they are often a burden to themselves; for, as Isaias says, [[Is 57:20|the wicked are like the raging sea, which cannot rest|Iniqui sunt quasi mare fervens, quod quiescere non potest]].

paras.t: Amplius, per hoc quod Deus ante inflictionem septimæ plagæ, tam terribiliter dixit, In hac vice mittam omnes plagas meas super cor tuum, etc., insinuatur quod Deus in se ipso invariabiliter dulcis, bonus et pius, per nimiam enormitatem et recidivationem frequentem, præsertim per rebellionem et obstinatam malitiam impiorum, quodammodo amaricatur et exacerbatur, dum per modum commoti se habens, amarissimas et abundantissimas punitiones infligit. Unde per istam terribilem commutationem et plagam hanc septimam, plura flagella in se comprehendentem, possunt intelligi signa, finale ac generale judicium præcessura. Imo ad litteram tunc erunt, ut legitur, tonitrua, fulgura, grandines, tempestates, imbres, et variæ impressiones copiosius ac terribilius, quam in Ægypto acciderant.
paras.en: Again, by this, that before inflicting the seventh plague God spoke so terribly, [[9:14|I will at this time send all my plagues upon thy heart|In hac vice mittam omnes plagas meas super cor tuum]], etc., it is intimated that God, who in Himself is unchangeably sweet, good and kind, is in a manner embittered and exasperated by the excessive enormity and frequent relapsing, above all by the rebellion and obstinate malice, of the wicked, when, bearing Himself after the manner of one who is moved, He inflicts most bitter and most abundant punishments. Hence by this terrible threat and by this seventh plague, which comprises several scourges in itself, may be understood the signs that will go before the last and general judgement. Nay, at that time there will literally be, as we read, thunders, lightnings, hailstorms, tempests, rains and various disturbances of the air [impressiones: the medieval term for things wrought in the sky and air, such as storms and meteors], more abundantly and more terribly than had happened in Egypt.

paras.t: Specialiter vero, per tonitrua accipiuntur clamorosæ et inordinatissimæ voces ac prædicationes hæreticorum et perfidorum ac schismaticorum, qui instar canum contra catholicæ fidei veritatem atque ecclesiasticam unitatem impudenter vociferantur ac perstrepunt, et argumenta sua quasi tonitrua magnipendunt: per fulgura quoque discurrentia, designantur reales et ignitæ persecutiones, quas undique contra Catholicos spargunt, et velocissime currere faciunt. Nam et materiali igne invadunt sacra loca atque fideles. Præsumunt etiam sententias excommunicationis quasi fulgura contra fideles emittere. Porro, per grandinem intelliguntur mortes amaræ, quas pro fide et justitia justis et fidelibus inferunt, sicut Salvator prædixit: Venit hora ut omnis qui interficit vos, arbitretur obsequium se præstare Deo. His plagis ac vitiis permittit iniquos Dominus lædi, spiritualiterque occidi. Quemadmodum etiam occisi sunt homines et jumenta non congregata in domum, ita qui in Ecclesia Christi non sunt fide et caritate uniti, dispereunt. Et si aliqua agunt bona ex genere, non tamen meritoria exstant, quia Christo incorporati non sunt, nec sunt viva Ecclesiæ membra.
paras.en: In particular, by the thunders are understood the clamorous and most disordered voices and preachings of heretics, of the faithless and of schismatics, who like dogs shamelessly shout and clamour against the truth of the Catholic faith and the unity of the Church, and make as much of their arguments as if they were thunders; by the lightnings running about, too, are designated the real and fiery persecutions which they scatter on every side against Catholics and make to run most swiftly. For they even attack holy places and the faithful with material fire. They also presume to hurl sentences of excommunication like lightnings against the faithful. Further, by the hail are understood the bitter deaths which they inflict on the just and faithful for the faith and for justice, as the Saviour foretold: [[John 16:2|the hour cometh, that whosoever killeth you will think that he doth a service to God|Venit hora ut omnis qui interficit vos, arbitretur obsequium se præstare Deo]]. By these plagues and vices the Lord permits the wicked to be hurt and spiritually slain. And just as the men and beasts that were not gathered into the house were slain, so those who are not united in the Church of Christ by faith and charity perish. And if they do some works that are good in their kind [bona ex genere: acts good by their object, though not done in grace], yet these are not meritorious, because they are not incorporated in Christ, nor are they living members of the Church.

paras.t: Postremo per hoc, quod magi et sapientes Pharaonis gravius læsi sunt sexta plaga, hoc innuit, quod in populo christiano multi sunt ingeniosi et humano studio eruditi, qui tamen juxta scientiam et doctrinam suam non conversantur, quales et in veteri Testamento Scribæ et Pharisæi fuerunt: ideo illi acrius relinquuntur et condemnantur a Deo. Scienti enim bonum facere, et non facienti, peccatum est illi. Propter quod asserit Christus : Servus qui cognovit voluntatem domini sui, et non fecit, plagis vapulabit multis.
paras.en: Lastly, by this, that the magicians and wise men of Pharao were more grievously hurt by the sixth plague, it is hinted that among the Christian people there are many who are clever and learned by human study, yet do not live according to their knowledge and teaching, such as the Scribes and Pharisees were in the Old Testament too: therefore these are the more sharply abandoned and condemned by God. For to him [[Jas 4:17|who knoweth to do good and doth it not, to him it is sin|Scienti enim bonum facere, et non facienti, peccatum est illi]] [the margin note here is lost; the words are James 4:17]. Therefore Christ declares: [[Luke 12:47|servant, who knew the will of his lord|Servus qui cognovit voluntatem domini sui]], [[Luke 12:47|and did not|et non fecit]], [[Luke 12:47|shall be beaten with many stripes|plagis vapulabit multis]] [Denis shortens the verse].

10.title: Expositio litteralis capituli decimi: Et dixit Dominus ad Moysen: Ingredere ad Pharaonem
10.title_en: Literal exposition of the tenth chapter: And the Lord said to Moses: Go in to Pharao

paras.t: Octava et nona plagæ hic describuntur.
paras.en: The eighth and ninth plagues are described here.

paras.t: Et dixit Dominus ad Moysen: Ingredere ad Pharaonem. Ego enim induravi cor ejus et servorum illius, hoc est indurari permisi. Et quo ego benignior sum removendo cito ab eo plagas illatas, eo obstinatior redditur, utpote mea longanimitate et patientia prorsus abutens. Et quia sic induratus fuit, necesse fuit ut frequenter admoneretur. Ut faciam signa mea hæc in eo, etc. Qualiter intelligendum sit hoc, constat ex dictis in præcedenti articulo super illud, Idcirco posui te, ut ostendam in te fortitudinem meam, etc. Circa hoc loquitur Augustinus: Hæc ita sonant, quasi Deus indigeat alicujus malitia ad ostendendum potentiam suam, seu rigorem justitiæ. Sed sic intelligendum est, quasi Dominus diceret: Ego patiens fui circa eum et servos ipsius, ne eos delerem, et hoc ordine superveniant signa mea in eos. Quia enim obstinatior fiebat malus animus ex patientia mea, dictum est, Induravi cor ejus.
paras.en: [[10:1|And the Lord said to Moses: Go in to Pharao|Et dixit Dominus ad Moysen: Ingredere ad Pharaonem]]. [[10:1|for I have hardened his heart, and the heart of his servants|Ego enim induravi cor ejus et servorum illius]], that is, I permitted them to be hardened. And the kinder I am in quickly taking away from him the plagues brought upon him, the more obstinate he becomes, utterly abusing my long-suffering and patience. And because he was hardened in this way, he had to be warned often. [[10:1|that I may work these my signs in him|Ut faciam signa mea hæc in eo]], etc. How this is to be understood is plain from what was said in the preceding article on the words, [[Ex 9:16|therefore have I raised thee, that I may shew my power in thee|Idcirco posui te, ut ostendam in te fortitudinem meam]], etc. On this Augustine says: These words sound as if God needed someone's malice to show his power, or the rigour of his justice. But it is to be understood as though the Lord said: I have been patient with him and his servants, so as not to destroy them, and in this order let my signs come upon them. For because the wicked mind grew more obstinate through my patience, it is said, [[10:1|I have hardened his heart|Induravi cor ejus]].

paras.t: Introierunt ergo Moyses et Aaron ad Pharaonem, et dixerunt ei: Hæc dicit Dominus Deus Hebræorum: Usquequo non vis subjici mihi? Dimitte populum meum, etc. Ecce ego inducam cras locustam in fines tuos, hoc est copiosissimam multitudinem locustarum in terram Ægypti, quæ operiet superficiem terræ, ne quidquam ejus appareat: id est, tot et tantæ erant locustæ in terra tua, ut juxta hyperbolicum modum loquendi, terra dicatur et videatur totaliter locustis operta; sed comedatur a locustis quod residuum fuit grandini, hoc est quod grando non destruxit in toto, prout dictum est præcedenti capitulo. Corrodet enim omnia ligna quæ germinant, id est fructum producunt, in agris aut hortis, id est, fructum arborum devorabunt. Et implebunt domos tuas et servorum tuorum et omnium Ægyptiorum: sicque et ipsos Ægyptios molestaverunt: quantum non viderunt patres tui, id est, tanta erit copia locustarum, quod nullus patrum tuorum vidit tam multas. Locusta, secundum Strabum, quoniam longiora habet retro crura, vocatur locusta, quasi longa hasta. Est tamen bestiola brevis et modica. Avertitque se Moyses et egressus est a Pharaone. Forsan ex zelo justitiæ indignabatur obstinatissimæ voluntati impii regis, ideoque recessit ab eo. Vel vidit per certa indicia, quod Pharao noluit obtemperare.
paras.en: [[10:3|Therefore Moses and Aaron went in to Pharao, and said to him: Thus saith the Lord God of the Hebrews: How long refusest thou to submit to me? let my people go|Introierunt ergo Moyses et Aaron ad Pharaonem, et dixerunt ei: Hæc dicit Dominus Deus Hebræorum: Usquequo non vis subjici mihi? Dimitte populum meum]], etc. [[10:4|behold I will bring in to-morrow the locusts into thy coasts|Ecce ego inducam cras locustam in fines tuos]], that is, a most abundant multitude of locusts into the land of Egypt, [[10:5|To cover the face of the earth, that nothing thereof may appear|quæ operiet superficiem terræ, ne quidquam ejus appareat]]: that is, the locusts in thy land shall be so many and so great that, by a hyperbolic manner of speaking, the land is said, and seen, to be wholly covered with locusts; [[10:5|but that which the hail hath left|quod residuum fuit grandini]] [[10:5|may be eaten|sed comedatur]] by the locusts: that is, what the hail did not wholly destroy, as was said in the preceding chapter[[Ex 9:32||]]. [[10:5|for they shall feed upon all the trees that spring|Corrodet enim omnia ligna quæ germinant]], that is, bear fruit, [[10:5|in the fields|in agris]] or gardens: that is, they will devour the fruit of the trees. [[10:6|And they shall fill thy houses, and the houses of thy servants, and of all the Egyptians|Et implebunt domos tuas et servorum tuorum et omnium Ægyptiorum]]: and so they troubled the Egyptians themselves too: [[10:6|such a number as thy fathers have not seen|quantum non viderunt patres tui]], that is, so great will be the abundance of locusts that none of thy fathers saw so many. The locust, according to Strabo, is called *locusta* because it has longer legs behind, as if *longa hasta* ["long spear": a play on the name]. Yet it is a short and small creature. [[10:6|And he turned himself away, and went forth from Pharao|Avertitque se Moyses et egressus est a Pharaone]]. Perhaps out of zeal for justice he was indignant at the most obstinate will of the wicked king, and therefore left him. Or he saw by sure signs that Pharao would not obey.

paras.t: Dixerunt autem servi Pharaonis ad eum: Usquequo patiemur hoc scandalum? hoc est, quamdiu sustinebimus has confusibiles plagas, per quas non solum affligimur, sed etiam diffamamur tanquam victi et infortunati ac miseri? Dimitte homines, ut sacrificent Domino Deo suo. Revocaveruntque Moysen et Aaron ad Pharaonem. Qui, scilicet Pharao, dixit eis: Ite, sacrificate Deo vestro. Quinam sunt, qui ituri sunt in desertum viam trium dierum? Ait Moyses: Cum parvulis nostris et senioribus pergemus, cum filiis et filiabus, cum ovibus et armentis, id est pecorum multitudinibus. Est enim solennitas Domini Dei nostri: idcirco oportet nos omnes adesse. Cur ita locutus sit Moyses, et qualiter hæc verba a mendacio excusentur, patet partim ex præinductis. Deus quippe in monte Sinai prædixerat Moysi, quod post egressum de Ægypto, immolaturus esset ei in monte illo: et diem in quo id erat implendum, vocat nunc Moyses Dei solennitatem, in qua Deus voluit omnes adesse Hebræos. Vel solennitatem Dei appellat, celebrem ejus venerationem, per sacrificia illa.
paras.en: [[10:7|And Pharao's servants said to him: How long shall we endure this scandal?|Dixerunt autem servi Pharaonis ad eum: Usquequo patiemur hoc scandalum?]] that is, how long shall we bear these shameful plagues, by which we are not only afflicted but also defamed as beaten, unfortunate and wretched? [[10:7|Iet the men go to sacrifice to the Lord their God|Dimitte homines, ut sacrificent Domino Deo suo]]. [[10:8|And they called back Moses, and Aaron, to Pharao|Revocaveruntque Moysen et Aaron ad Pharaonem]]. He, that is, Pharao, [[10:8|said to them: Go, sacrifice to the Lord your God|dixit eis: Ite, sacrificate Deo vestro]]. [[10:8|who are they that shall go|Quinam sunt, qui ituri sunt]] into the desert, three days' journey? [[10:9|Moses said: We will go with our young and old, with our sons and daughters, with our sheep and herds|Ait Moyses: Cum parvulis nostris et senioribus pergemus, cum filiis et filiabus, cum ovibus et armentis]], that is, with multitudes of cattle. [[10:9|for it is the solemnity of the Lord our God|Est enim solennitas Domini Dei nostri]]: therefore we must all be there. Why Moses spoke so, and how these words are cleared of a lie, is partly plain from what was set out earlier. For God had foretold to Moses on Mount Sinai that after the going out from Egypt he would sacrifice to him on that mountain; and the day on which this was to be fulfilled Moses now calls the solemnity of God, at which God willed all the Hebrews to be present. Or he calls the solemn worship of him by those sacrifices the solemnity of God.

paras.t: Et respondit Pharao: Sic Dominus sit vobiscum, quomodo ego dimittam vos et parvulos vestros. Aspernatorie atque ironice, imo et negative ac invidialiter dixit hoc, tanquam dicat: Sicut ego non dimittam vos ac filios vestros, sic Dominus non sit vobiscum. Et quamvis Moyses non solum expresserat parvulos, sed etiam senes et filios ac filias, oves atque armenta. Pharao tamen non repetit nisi parvulos, hoc est infantulos, sciens quod parentes invitissime desererent suos infantes; vel quia ex nominatione parvulorum, magis suspicabatur fallaciam: nam et infantium præsentiam in sacrificio minus necessariam reputavit. Ideo subdit: Cui dubium est quod pessime cogitetis? quasi dicat: Certum est cunctis hæc audientibus, quod nos decipere vultis, nec reverti intenditis, aut etiam repugnare et insidiari nobis disponitis. Quæ omnia Pharao pessima judicavit. Hinc primo libri hujus capitulo fertur dixisse: Ecce populus filiorum Israel multus, et fortior nobis est. Venite, sapienter opprimamus eum, ne forte multiplicetur, et si ingruerit contra nos bellum, addatur inimicis nostris, expugnatisque nobis, egrediatur de terra. Non fiet ita, sed ite tantum viri, et sacrificate Domino: quoniam certum est, quod uxores vestras ac sobolem non relinquetis in terra. Hoc enim et ipsi petistis. Forsitan Pharao æstimavit, quod Moyses et Aaron non intenderent petere exeundi et sacrificandi licentiam, nisi pro viris dumtaxat. Non tamen oportet eum in verbis his a mendacio excusare. Statimque ejecti sunt de conspectu Pharaonis: hoc est, quum Moyses et Aaron non fuissent contenti de ista Pharaonis licentia, tam ipse rex quam ejus ministri contra Moysen et Aaron indignabantur, et rege jubente, ministri cum ira et aspernatione fecerunt eos exire.
paras.en: [[10:10|And Pharao answered: So be the Lord with you, as I shall let you and your children go|Et respondit Pharao: Sic Dominus sit vobiscum, quomodo ego dimittam vos et parvulos vestros]]. He said this scornfully and ironically, indeed as a refusal and with ill will, as if to say: As I shall not let you and your sons go, so may the Lord not be with you. And although Moses had named not only the little ones but also the old, and the sons and daughters, the sheep and the herds, Pharao repeats only the little ones, that is, the infants, knowing that the parents would be most unwilling to leave their infants behind; or because from the naming of the little ones he suspected deceit the more, for he thought the presence of infants at a sacrifice less necessary. So he adds: [[10:10|who can doubt but that you intend some great evil?|Cui dubium est quod pessime cogitetis?]] as if to say: It is certain to all who hear this that you mean to deceive us and do not intend to come back, or even that you are planning to resist us and lay snares for us. All of which Pharao judged most evil. Hence in the first chapter of this book he is said to have said: [[Ex 1:9|Behold the people of the children of Israel are numerous and stronger than we|Ecce populus filiorum Israel multus, et fortior nobis est]]. [[Ex 1:10|Come let us wisely oppress them, lest they multiply: and if any war shall rise against us, join with our enemies, and having overcome us, depart out of the land|Venite, sapienter opprimamus eum, ne forte multiplicetur, et si ingruerit contra nos bellum, addatur inimicis nostris, expugnatisque nobis, egrediatur de terra]]. [[10:11|It shall not be so. but go ye men only, and sacrifice to the Lord|Non fiet ita, sed ite tantum viri, et sacrificate Domino]]: since it is certain that you will not leave your wives and offspring in the land. [[10:11|for this yourselves also desired|Hoc enim et ipsi petistis]]. Perhaps Pharao thought that Moses and Aaron did not mean to ask leave to go out and sacrifice except for the men only. Yet there is no need to clear him of a lie in these words. [[10:11|And immediately they were cast out from Pharao's presence|Statimque ejecti sunt de conspectu Pharaonis]]: that is, since Moses and Aaron were not content with this leave of Pharao's, both the king himself and his ministers were indignant against Moses and Aaron, and at the king's bidding the ministers made them go out with anger and scorn.

paras.t: Dixit autem Dominus ad Moysen, quum fuisset ejectus, die eodem vel sequente: Extende manum tuam super terram Ægypti ad locustam, ut ascendat super eam, hoc est, ad hoc ut ego faciam multitudinem locustarum venire. Superius dictum est, quod Moyses jussus est manum extendere versus cœlum, quoniam fuit in his quæ sunt ad Deum: Aaron vero super terram, quia in his quæ erant ad populum, fuerat medius constitutus. Cur ergo nunc præcipit Dominus Moysi, ut manum super terram extendat? Ad hoc Augustinus respondet: Dictum est Moysi, Extende manum tuam in cœlum, nec unquam hoc dictum est Aaron. Quod ergo nunc dicitur Moysi, Extende manum tuam super terram, hoc credo significare, quod is qui potest quod majus est, possit quoque quod minus est, non econverso: quod verum est in potestatibus subordinatis, in quantum hujusmodi. Extendit Moyses virgam super terram Ægypti. Per hoc constat, quod manum simul cum virga super terram levavit, in signum quod Dominus terram fuerat percussurus. Dominus autem, cujus dignatio est immensa in suis electis, quamvis per se ipsum omnia possit, in aliquibus tamen vult homines habere quasi cooperatores. Propter quod ait Apostolus: Dei adjutores sumus. Et Dominus induxit ventum urentem, id est valde calidum: et forsan fuit ventus australis, qui et naturaliter calidus est, sed tunc ultra solitum calidus fuit et siccus: tota die illa qua Moyses manum levavit. Quod intelligitur de die artificiali, qui est pars diei naturalis. Nam subditur, et nocte. Fuitque ventus ille dispositivus ad generationem et multiplicationem locustarum.
paras.en: [[10:12|And the Lord said to Moses|Dixit autem Dominus ad Moysen]], when he had been cast out, on the same day or the next: [[10:12|Stretch forth thy hand upon the land of Egypt unto the locust, that it come upon it|Extende manum tuam super terram Ægypti ad locustam, ut ascendat super eam]], that is, so that I may make a multitude of locusts come. It was said above that Moses was commanded to stretch out his hand towards heaven, since he was set over the things that are towards God, but Aaron over the earth, since he had been appointed the go-between in the things that were towards the people. Why then does the Lord now command Moses to stretch out his hand over the land? To this Augustine answers: It was said to Moses, [[Ex 9:22|Stretch forth thy hand towards heaven|Extende manum tuam in cœlum]], and this was never said to Aaron. That it is now said to Moses, [[10:12|Stretch forth thy hand upon the land|Extende manum tuam super terram]], signifies, I believe, that he who can do the greater can also do the lesser, but not the other way round: which is true of subordinate powers, as such. [[10:13|And Moses stretched forth his rod upon the land of Egypt|Extendit Moyses virgam super terram Ægypti]]. From this it is plain that he raised his hand together with the rod over the land, as a sign that the Lord was about to strike the land. Now the Lord, whose condescension towards his elect is boundless, though he can do all things by himself, yet in some things wills to have men as it were his fellow workers. Wherefore the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 3:9|we are God's coadjutors|Dei adjutores sumus]]. [[10:13|and the Lord brought a burning wind|Et Dominus induxit ventum urentem]], that is, a very hot one: and perhaps it was the south wind, which is hot by nature too, but was then hot and dry beyond its wont, [[10:13|all that day|tota die illa]] on which Moses raised his hand. This is understood of the artificial day [that is, the hours of daylight], which is part of the natural day [of twenty-four hours]. For there follows, [[10:13|and night|et nocte]]. And that wind made things ready for the breeding and multiplying of the locusts.

paras.t: Et mane facto, ventus urens levavit locustas de superficie terræ in qua erant natæ, ita quod volare cœperunt. Ideo subditur: quæ ascenderunt super universam terram Ægypti, et sederunt in cunctis finibus Ægyptiorum: ex quo videtur, quod etiam alibi natæ, illuc venerunt: innumerabiles, quales ante tempus illud non fuerunt in terra Ægypti aut etiam alibi, nec postea futuræ sunt. Hoc prophetico spiritu Moyses protulit, quia nec aliter scire id poterat, maxime quod nec postea tot essent locustæ simul venturæ in terra. Quod si intelligatur de tota terra habitabili, potest habere instantiam ex eo quod in Joele habetur: Audite hoc, habitatores terræ, si factum est istud in diebus vestris, aut in diebus patrum vestrorum? Residuum erucæ comedit locusta, et residuum locustæ comedit bruchus, et residuum bruchi comedit ærugo. In quibus verbis capitur si, pro non. Ad hoc breviter dici potest, quod Joel non loquitur de multitudine locustarum, sicut nunc Moyses, sed de successiva illa devoratione. Hieronymus quoque super Joelem, per erucam, locustam, et bruchum intelligit diversas gentes ad litteram, quæ vastarunt Hebræos. Et idem dicit sentire Judæos, ut plenius scripsi ibidem. Alii dicunt, quod plaga locustarum, de qua nunc sermo, fuit gravior intensive, quam plaga de qua loquitur Joel, quam dicunt fuisse ista majorem extensive seu diuturnitate.
paras.en: [[10:13|and when it was morning, the burning wind raised the locusts|Et mane facto, ventus urens levavit locustas]] from the face of the earth on which they had been born, so that they began to fly. So it is added: [[10:14|And they came up over the whole land of Egypt; and rested in all the coasts of the Egyptians|quæ ascenderunt super universam terram Ægypti, et sederunt in cunctis finibus Ægyptiorum]]: from which it seems that locusts born elsewhere also came there: [[10:14|innumerable, the like as had not been before that time|innumerabiles, quales ante tempus illud non fuerunt]] in the land of Egypt, or anywhere else either, [[10:14|nor shall be hereafter|nec postea futuræ sunt]]. Moses uttered this by the spirit of prophecy, since he could not have known it otherwise, above all that never afterwards would so many locusts come together upon the earth. But if this is understood of the whole habitable earth, an objection can be raised against it [Latin *instantia*, the schoolmen's word for a counter-instance] from what is found in Joel: [[Joel 1:2|Hear this|Audite hoc]], [[Joel 1:2|ye inhabitants of the land: did this ever happen in your days, or in the days of your fathers?|habitatores terræ, si factum est istud in diebus vestris, aut in diebus patrum vestrorum?]] [[Joel 1:4|That which the palmerworm hath left, the locust hath eaten: and that which the locust hath left, the bruchus hath eaten: and that which the bruchus hath left, the mildew hath destroyed|Residuum erucæ comedit locusta, et residuum locustæ comedit bruchus, et residuum bruchi comedit ærugo]]. In these words *if* is taken for *not* [the Latin reads *si factum est istud*, literally "if this has been done", meaning "this has never been done"]. To this it may briefly be said that Joel is not speaking of the multitude of the locusts, as Moses is here, but of that devouring of one after another. Jerome too, on Joel, understands by the palmerworm, the locust and the bruchus, in the literal sense, various nations which laid waste the Hebrews; and he says that the Jews think the same, as I have written more fully there. Others say that the plague of locusts now spoken of was the more severe in intensity than the plague of which Joel speaks, which they say was greater than this one in extent, or in duration.

paras.t: Devorata est ergo herba terræ, et quidquid pomorum in arboribus fuit. Nomine pomi solet in Scripturis quicumque arborum fructus significari. Et ita nunc accipi potest.
paras.en: [[10:15|And the grass of the earth was devoured, and what fruits soever were on the trees|Devorata est ergo herba terræ, et quidquid pomorum in arboribus fuit]]. By the name *pomum* [the word rendered "fruits" here; often an apple] any fruit of trees is usually meant in the Scriptures, and so it can be taken here.

paras.t: Quamobrem festinus Pharao vocavit Moysen et Aaron, et dixit eis: Peccavi in Dominum Deum vestrum, ejus præcepta toties contemnendo, et ejus beneficiis exsistendo ingratus: et in vos, quos indignanter ejeci, et contumeliose affatus sum, et contempsi; sed nunc dimittite peccatum mihi etiam hac vice, et rogate Dominum Deum vestrum, ut auferat a me et a populo meo mortem istam, id est plagam istam, duram ut morti similis videatur: et aliquos læsit forsitan usque ad mortem. Egressusque Moyses oravit Dominum. Qui flare fecit ventum ab occidente: fuitque ventus ille frigidus et debilitativus locustarum, sicut ventus australis calidus eas fortificavit; vehementissimum; et arreptam locustam, hoc est totam earum multitudinem, projecit in mare Rubrum impetu suo tam valido et acuto.
paras.en: [[10:16|Wherefore Pharao in haste called Moses and Aaron, and said to them: I have sinned against the Lord your God|Quamobrem festinus Pharao vocavit Moysen et Aaron, et dixit eis: Peccavi in Dominum Deum vestrum]], by despising his commandments so many times, and by being ungrateful for his benefits: [[10:16|and against you|et in vos]], whom I cast out in indignation, and spoke to insultingly, and despised. [[10:17|But now forgive me my sin this time also, and pray to the Lord your God|sed nunc dimittite peccatum mihi etiam hac vice, et rogate Dominum Deum vestrum]], [[10:17|that he take away from me|ut auferat a me]] and from my people [[10:17|this death|mortem istam]], that is, this plague, so hard that it seems like death: and perhaps it hurt some even to death. [[10:18|And Moses going forth|Egressusque Moyses]] [[10:18|prayed to the Lord|oravit Dominum]]. [[10:19|And he made a very strong wind to blow from the west|Qui flare fecit ventum ab occidente]]: and that wind was cold, and weakened the locusts, as the hot south wind had strengthened them; [[10:19|and it took the locusts|et arreptam locustam]], that is, their whole multitude, and [[10:19|cast them into the Red Sea|projecit in mare Rubrum]] by its so strong and sharp onset.

paras.t: Sequitur plaga nona. Dixit autem Dominus ad Moysen: Extende manum tuam in cælum cum virga tua. In hac plaga non legitur Deus præavisasse Pharaonem per Moysen ob nimiam ejus duritiam. Et sint tenebræ super terram Ægypti tam densæ, ut palpari queant. Extenditque Moyses manum in cælum, et factæ sunt tenebræ horribiles in universa terra Ægypti. Tribus diebus nemo vidit fratrem suum, nec movit se de loco in quo erat, id est, nullus Ægyptiorum vidit proximum suum. Quo constat, quod triduo duravit illa caligo. Porro tenebræ, quum non sint proprie aliquid positivum, sed privatio luminis tantum, proprie non valent palpari: idcirco per hoc quod dicuntur potuisse palpari, hyperbolice designatur magnitudo earum. Vel, per palpabilitatem tenebrarum insinuatur, quod aer qui in Ægypto naturaliter clarus est ac subtilis, fuit tunc taliter ingrossatus, vaporibusque repletus, quod quivit palpari. Erant quoque tenebræ illæ horribiles, incutiendo terrorem Ægyptiis; atque ut dicitur, apparitiones imaginariæ terribiles in triduo illo fiebant Ægyptiis: imo ut in Scholastica fertur historia, multi Ægyptiorum coacti sunt tunc mirabiliter ac miserabiliter mori. Recitat etiam Lyra, quod secundum Hebræos, tunc moriebantur et quidam increduli ac perversi ex filiis Israel, qui noluerunt exire Ægyptum. Unde et Deus tunc induxit caliginem etiam ob hoc, ne Ægyptii hoc cognoscerent, et inter se dicerent, Ita percussi sunt Hebræi, sicut et nos, et mortem Hebræorum diis propriis adscripsissent.
paras.en: The ninth plague follows. [[10:21|And the Lord said to Moses: Stretch out thy hand towards heaven|Dixit autem Dominus ad Moysen: Extende manum tuam in cælum]] with thy rod. In this plague we do not read that God forewarned Pharao through Moses, because of his excessive hardness. [[10:21|and may there be darkness upon the land of Egypt so thick that it may be felt|Et sint tenebræ super terram Ægypti tam densæ, ut palpari queant]]. [[10:22|And Moses stretched forth his hand towards heaven: and there came horrible darkness in all the land of Egypt for three days|Extenditque Moyses manum in cælum, et factæ sunt tenebræ horribiles in universa terra Ægypti. Tribus diebus]] [[10:23|No man saw his brother, nor moved himself out of the place where he was|nemo vidit fratrem suum, nec movit se de loco in quo erat]], that is, none of the Egyptians saw his neighbour. From this it is plain that that darkness lasted three days. Now darkness, since it is not properly anything positive but only a privation of light, cannot properly be felt: so by its being said that it could be felt, its greatness is signified by hyperbole. Or by the darkness being palpable it is suggested that the air, which in Egypt is naturally clear and thin, was then so thickened and filled with vapours that it could be felt. That darkness was also horrible, striking terror into the Egyptians; and, as is said, terrible imaginary apparitions came upon the Egyptians in those three days; indeed, as is related in the *Scholastic History* [of Peter Comestor], many of the Egyptians were then made to die in a wondrous and pitiable way. Lyra also relates that, according to the Hebrews, some unbelieving and perverse men of the children of Israel, who would not go out of Egypt, died at that time too. And so God brought on the darkness then for this reason also, that the Egyptians might not know of it and say among themselves, The Hebrews are struck just as we are, and so ascribe the death of the Hebrews to their own gods.

paras.t: Ubicumque autem habitabant filii Israel, lux erat tempore opportuno. Hinc Damascenus et doctores catholici dicunt communiter, quod signum istud tam admirabile fuit per hoc, quod omnipotente Creatore jubente, sol radios suos subtraxit, seu non effudit super terram habitationis Ægyptiorum; sed super terram mansionis Hebræorum, solito modo lumen effudit. Verumtamen indensatio aeris, et vaporum grossities, poterant ad obscurationem illam Ægyptiis factam, cooperari. Dicendum quoque, quod nec stellæ, neque planetæ aliquid luminis influxerunt terræ Ægyptiorum infra triduum illud. Verumtamen Rabbi Paulus circa hæc aliter sentit, dicens quod aer fuit tunc tam vehementer ingrossatus, quod diaphaneitatem suam amisit, nec luminis capax erat. Quod probat dupliciter: Primo, nam aliter potuissent Ægyptii se videre per lampades et lucernas. Secundo, quoniam infra tres dies nemo se movit de loco in quo erat, ut in textu habetur. Ideo dicit quod sol consueto modo lumen effudit, sed aer qui circa Ægyptios fuit, non erat capax illius. Verum ut tactum est, istud non consonat dictis catholicorum doctorum, nec apparentiam habet. Si enim aer fuisset sic ingrossatus, quod nullus Ægyptiorum potuisset locum mutare, tunc aer suam amisisset mollitiem, et durior fuisset spissiorque quam aqua, nec aliquis Ægyptiorum infra triduum illud fuisset usus cibo aut potu. Glossa etiam dicit super illud, Nec movit se, etc.: Non quod penitus non moveretur, sed quia de loco ad locum migrare non poterant. Hinc verior reputatur expositio catholicorum doctorum. Secunda quoque ratio Rabbi Pauli soluta est, quoniam falsum supponit. Ad primam vero rationem ejus respondetur, quod indispositio, humefactio aut turbulentia aeris, aut simile aliquid, accensionem luminarium poterat impedire: quod et divina virtute fieri poterat. Nam et in adventu tenebrarum illarum, ignes Ægyptiorum videntur exstincti, vel vi illuminativa privati. Nec incredibile, Deum abstulisse tunc vim illuminandi terrenis luminaribus Ægyptiorum, qui cœlestibus luminaribus abstulit solitam influentiam luminis super Ægyptios.
paras.en: [[10:23|but wheresoever the children of Israel dwelt, there was light|Ubicumque autem habitabant filii Israel, lux erat]] at the proper time. Hence Damascene and the catholic doctors commonly say that this so wonderful sign came about thus: at the bidding of the almighty Creator, the sun withdrew its rays from, or did not pour them out upon, the land where the Egyptians lived, but upon the land where the Hebrews dwelt it poured out its light in the usual way. Yet the thickening of the air and the grossness of the vapours could have helped towards that darkening brought on the Egyptians. It must be said too that neither the stars nor the planets shed any light upon the land of the Egyptians during those three days. Rabbi Paul [Paul of Burgos, a converted rabbi, author of the Additions to Lyra], however, thinks otherwise about this, saying that the air was then so violently thickened that it lost its transparency and could not take in light. He proves this in two ways: first, because otherwise the Egyptians could have seen one another by lamps and candles; secondly, because for three days no one moved from the place where he was, as the text has it. So he says that the sun poured out its light in the usual way, but the air about the Egyptians could not take it in. But, as was touched on, this does not agree with what the catholic doctors say, nor is it likely. For if the air had been so thickened that none of the Egyptians could change his place, then the air would have lost its softness and been harder and denser than water, and none of the Egyptians could have taken food or drink during those three days. The Gloss too says on the words, [[10:23|nor moved himself|Nec movit se]], etc.: Not that they did not move at all, but that they could not pass from place to place. Hence the exposition of the catholic doctors is held to be the truer. Rabbi Paul's second reason is also answered, since it supposes what is false. To his first reason it is answered that an unfit state of the air, its dampness or turbulence, or something of the kind, could hinder the kindling of lights; and this could also come about by the power of God. For at the coming of that darkness the fires of the Egyptians seem to have been put out, or deprived of their power to give light. Nor is it incredible that God then took away the power of giving light from the earthly lights of the Egyptians, he who took away from the heavenly lights their wonted outpouring of light upon the Egyptians.

paras.t: Vocavitque Pharao Moysen et Aaron. Quæritur, qualiter eos vocavit et quando. Nam infra triduum illud, nullus Ægyptiorum poterat ire ad eos. Ad hoc communiter respondetur, quod post triduum illud luce reversa, vocavit eos timore majoris plagæ futuræ, sicut et post primogenitorum percussionem compulit Hebræos exire timore propriæ mortis et populi sui. Unde infra non habetur, quod rogavit hanc plagam tenebrarum auferri. Nec mirum quod duriorem timuit plagam, nisi dimitteret populum, quia jam toties fuit expertus novam et duriorem sibi plagam inflictam, eo quod præcedenti plaga sublata, non dimiserat eos. Et dixit eis: Ite, sacrificate Domino. Pharao verberibus eruditus, et aliqualiter humiliatus, eum didicit Dominum appellare, de quo ante dixit, Nescio Dominum. Oves tantum vestræ et armenta remaneant in Ægypto. Hoc addidit Pharao, quia timuit quod non redirent. Vel si non redirent, obtineret saltem jumenta ipsorum. Parvuli vestri eant vobiscum. Ait Moyses: Hostias quoque et holocausta dabis nobis, hoc est, permittes ut animalia nostra, ex quibus sacrificia offeremus, ducamus nobiscum. Cuncti greges pecorum nostrorum pergent nobiscum, etc.; præsertim quum ignoremus quid immolari debeat, donec ad ipsum locum sacrificii perveniamus. Hoc ideo protulit Moyses, quoniam Deus non expresserat ei in speciali, quid, quantum, et quoties fieret ei immolatio ab Hebræis. Verumtamen istud non fuit totalis principalisque causa, quod cuncta pecora irent cum eis, sed quod non fuerant redituri. Non tamen mentitus est Moyses, sed unam causam expressit, aliam tacuit, ut Pharao nullam excusationem suæ obstinationis haberet.
paras.en: [[10:24|And Pharao called Moses and Aaron|Vocavitque Pharao Moysen et Aaron]]. It is asked how and when he called them, for during those three days none of the Egyptians could go to them. To this the common answer is that after those three days, when the light had come back, he called them for fear of a greater plague to come; just as after the slaying of the firstborn he drove the Hebrews out for fear of his own death and his people's. Hence we do not find below that he asked for this plague of darkness to be taken away. Nor is it surprising that he feared a harder plague unless he let the people go, since he had already found so many times that a new and harder plague was laid on him because, when the plague before it was taken away, he had not let them go. [[10:24|and said to them: Go, sacrifice to the Lord|Et dixit eis: Ite, sacrificate Domino]]. Pharao, taught by stripes and somewhat humbled, learned to call him Lord of whom he had said before, [[Ex 5:2|I know not the Lord|Nescio Dominum]]. [[10:24|let your sheep only, and herds remain|Oves tantum vestræ et armenta remaneant]] in Egypt. Pharao added this because he feared they would not come back; or, if they did not come back, so that he might at least keep their beasts. [[10:24|let your children go with you|Parvuli vestri eant vobiscum]]. [[10:25|Moses said: Thou shalt give us also sacrifices and burnt-offerings|Ait Moyses: Hostias quoque et holocausta dabis nobis]], that is, thou shalt let us take with us our animals, from which we shall offer sacrifices. [[10:26|All the flocks|Cuncti greges]] of our cattle [[10:26|shall go with us|pergent nobiscum]], etc.; [[10:26|especially as we know not what must be offered, till we come to the very place|præsertim quum ignoremus quid immolari debeat, donec ad ipsum locum]] of sacrifice. Moses said this because God had not told him in particular what, how much, and how often the Hebrews were to sacrifice to him. Yet this was not the whole and chief reason why all the cattle were to go with them, but that they were not going to come back. Moses did not lie, however, but gave one reason and kept silent about another, so that Pharao should have no excuse for his obstinacy.

paras.t: Induravit autem Dominus cor Pharaonis, et noluit dimittere eos. Dixitque Pharao ad Moysen tanquam ad principalem. Tamen quod dixit ad eum, intendebat etiam ad Aaron dirigi. Cave ne ultra videas faciem meam: hoc est, ne amplius appareas coram me, ita ut videam te, nisi a tuo resipiscas proposito. Quocumque die apparueris mihi, morieris, hoc est occidi te faciam. Hoc solita temeritate et præsumptione protulit Pharao, quasi Deus qui tot et tanta miracula per Moysen fecerat, non potuerit eum coram Pharaone positum, liberare a morte. Respondit Moyses: Ita fiet ut locutus es. Non videbo ultra faciem tuam in hac vita. Verumtamen infra legitur, quod vocatis Moyse et Aaron Pharao dixit: Ite, egredimini de terra mea. Sed hoc fuit in nocte, et forte per internuntiis. Vel intentio Moysis fuit, quod ultra non videret Pharaonem, proprio motu eundo ad ipsum.
paras.en: [[10:27|And the Lord hardened Pharao's heart, and he would not let them go|Induravit autem Dominus cor Pharaonis, et noluit dimittere eos]]. [[10:28|And Pharao said to Moses|Dixitque Pharao ad Moysen]], as to the chief of the two; yet what he said to him he meant to be addressed to Aaron as well. [[10:28|beware thou see not my face any more|Cave ne ultra videas faciem meam]]: that is, do not appear before me any more, so that I see thee, unless thou come to thy senses and give up thy purpose. [[10:28|in what day soever thou shalt come in my sight, thou shalt die|Quocumque die apparueris mihi, morieris]], that is, I will have thee killed. Pharao said this with his usual rashness and presumption, as if God, who had worked so many and so great miracles through Moses, could not deliver him from death when he stood before Pharao. [[10:29|Moses answered: So shall it be as thou hast spoken, I will not see thy face anymore|Respondit Moyses: Ita fiet ut locutus es. Non videbo ultra faciem tuam]] in this life. Yet we read below that Pharao called Moses and Aaron and said: Go, depart out of my land[[Ex 12:31||]] [the margin's note is partly unreadable ("… 31"); the place is Ex 12:31, where the Douay-Rheims has: Arise and go forth from among my people]. But this was at night, and perhaps through messengers. Or Moses meant that he would see Pharao no more by going to him of his own accord.

paras.t: Postremo, densissimarum harum plaga tenebrarum, apertissime correspondet admirabili excæcationi Pharaonis et Ægyptiorum internæ et vitiosæ, qui post tot et tanta prodigia, in sua manserunt perfidia atque malitia.
paras.en: Lastly, this plague of the thickest darkness corresponds most plainly to the wondrous inward and sinful blindness of Pharao and the Egyptians, who after so many and so great wonders remained in their faithlessness and malice.

paras.t: At vero juxta intelligentiam spiritualem, per locustas recte accipiuntur simulatores, et callidi adulatores, et seductores magistri. Etenim Salomone testante, locusta quamvis regem non habeat, tamen per turmas egreditur universa. Sic præfati, qui etsi Christum non imitantur, tamen forinsecus quamdam ordinationem et honestatem simulant et assumunt. Et sicut locusta specialiter fructibus frugibusque noxia est, et quod superfuit grandini, devoravit; ita præfati miro et miserabili modo noxii sunt proximis suis, eos per detractiones, simulationes, adulationes, et falsas informationes inficiendo atque fallendo, in tantum, quod hi qui graves tentationes adversitatum, tanquam grandinum ictus vicerunt et evaserunt, per talium blandimenta et susurrationes ac suggestiones pestiferas, corrumpantur, bonorumque operum fructibus spolientur.
paras.en: But in the spiritual understanding, by the locusts are rightly meant dissemblers, and crafty flatterers, and masters who lead astray. For, as Solomon testifies, [[Prov 30:27|The locust hath no king, yet they all go out by their bands|locusta quamvis regem non habeat, tamen per turmas egreditur universa]]. So with the men just named: though they do not follow Christ [their King], yet outwardly they feign and put on a certain orderliness and uprightness. And as the locust is especially harmful to fruits and crops, and devoured what the hail had left, so these men are harmful to their neighbours in a strange and pitiable way, infecting and deceiving them by detractions, pretences, flatteries and false teachings; so much so that those who have overcome and escaped grave temptations of adversity, like the blows of hail, are corrupted by the blandishments, whisperings and pestilent suggestions of such men, and are stripped of the fruits of good works.

paras.t: Porro per densissimas atque palpabiles tenebras, designantur eorum qui vitiosis consuetudinibus pressi sunt, detestabiles et apertissimæ excæcationes interiores; qui nullam increpationem suscipiunt, nulli informationi acquiescunt, nulla compunctione emolliuntur, nec a sua pravitate flectuntur, imo in via perditionis quasi immobiliter stant, infeliciter obdurati, super quos puteus clausit os suum. Impii namque quum in profundum venerint peccatorum, contemnunt. Pro quibus jugiter est orandum, quia a solo cœlesti omnipotentique Medico possint curari.
paras.en: Further, by the thickest and palpable darkness is signified the hateful and most open inward blindness of those who are weighed down by sinful habits; who accept no rebuke, give way to no instruction, are softened by no compunction, and are not turned from their wickedness, but stand as it were immovable in the way of perdition, unhappily hardened, those upon whom [[Ps 68:16|the pit shut her mouth|puteus clausit os suum]]. For [[Prov 18:3|The wicked man, when he is come into the depths of sins, contemneth|Impii namque quum in profundum venerint peccatorum, contemnunt]]. For such we must pray without ceasing, since they can be cured only by the heavenly and almighty Physician.

11.title: Explanatio capituli undecimi: Et dixit Dominus ad Moysen
11.title_en: Explanation of the eleventh chapter: And the Lord said to Moses

paras.t: Justus et pius Deus, in omni opere suo misericordiam justitiamque contemperat. Sic et nunc inflicturus Ægyptiis decimam plagam præhabitis graviorem, primo præavisat Ægyptios. Et dixit Dominus ad Moysen. Ista allocutio facta est Moysi antequam a Pharaone recessit, sicut ex sequentibus innotescit : imo et facta videtur Moysi coram Pharaone adhuc stante, per illuminationem internam, vel angelicam apparitionem, soli Moysi demonstratam. Interdum quippe revelationes propheticæ et illuminationes divinæ, factæ sunt viris sanctis in aliorum præsentia, aut etiam coram iniquis hominibus. Unde, ut legitur libro quarto Regum, facta est prophetalis revelatio Eliseo coram tribus regibus cum exercitibus suis, quorum unus exstitit justus, videlicet Josaphat, alii duo injusti, utputa Joram rex Israel, et rex Edom. Secundo quoque Paralipomenon legitur, quemadmodum ipso Josaphat et habitatoribus Jerusalem in templo stantibus, factus est spiritus Domini super Jahaziel, et prophetavit.
paras.en: God, just and loving, tempers mercy and justice together in all His work. So now too, when He is about to inflict on the Egyptians the tenth plague, heavier than those that went before, He first forewarns the Egyptians. [[11:1|And the Lord said to Moses|Et dixit Dominus ad Moysen]]. This address was made to Moses before he left Pharao, as appears from what follows; indeed it seems to have been made to Moses while he was still standing before Pharao, by an inward enlightenment or by the appearance of an angel shown to Moses alone. For prophetic revelations and divine enlightenments have at times been given to holy men in the presence of others, or even before wicked men. Thus, as we read in the fourth book of Kings, a prophetic revelation was given to Eliseus before three kings with their armies, of whom one was just, namely Josaphat, and the other two unjust, that is, Joram king of Israel and the king of Edom[[4 Kings 3:15||]] [the margin gives IV Reg. iii, 15–19]. And in the second book of Paralipomenon we read how, while Josaphat himself and the inhabitants of Jerusalem were standing in the temple, [[2 Par 20:14|the spirit of the Lord came|factus est spiritus Domini]] upon Jahaziel, and he prophesied.

paras.t: Sequitur : Adhuc una plaga tangam Pharaonem et Ægyptium, hoc est Ægyptios. Plaga hæc, fuit interfectio primogenitorum in hominibus et jumentis : quæ quamvis non tetigit immediate Pharaonis et omnium Ægyptiorum personas, tetigit eos tamen mediate, quia redundavit in eos, et afflictiva fuit eorum ; et post hæc dimittet vos cum sobole atque pecoribus vestris, et exire compellet timore propriæ occisionis. Non autem sic compulit, quod filii Israel exierunt invite ; sed compulit, id est, importune ac festinanter excitavit seu provocavit ad exeundum : quod et Hebræi libenter fecerunt. Dices ergo omni plebi Hebræorum, ut postulet vir ab amico suo, id est, ut viri Hebræi postulent ab Ægyptiis sibi amicabilibus, et mulier a vicina sua, hoc est mulier Hebræa ab Ægyptiis feminis juxta se commorantibus, vasa argentea et aurea ; et etiam vestem plurimam, seu multiplicia vestimenta, ut sequenti habetur capitulo. Dabit autem Dominus gratiam populo suo coram Ægyptiis, id est, corda Ægyptiorum inclinabit ad hoc, ut bene afficiantur circa Hebræos, et faveant atque accommodent eis vasa ac vestes. Hic variatur modus loquendi de prima persona in tertiam. Nempe quum dixisset Dominus ad Moysen in prima persona, Adhuc una plaga tangam Pharaonem ; nunc in tertia persona adjicitur, Dabit autem Dominus gratiam. Itaque angelus qui verba illa in prima persona protulit, quasi loquens in Dei persona, ista verba in tertia persona locutus est in propria persona de Deo, sicut de alio.
paras.en: There follows: [[11:1|Yet one plague more will I bring upon Pharao and Egypt|Adhuc una plaga tangam Pharaonem et Ægyptium]], that is, the Egyptians [Denis reads *Ægyptium*, "the Egyptian", where the Vulgate has *Ægyptum*, "Egypt", and takes it of the Egyptians as a whole]. This plague was the slaying of the firstborn among men and beasts: and although it did not touch the persons of Pharao and of all the Egyptians directly, it touched them indirectly, because it fell back upon them and was an affliction to them. [[11:1|and after that he shall let you go|et post hæc dimittet vos]] with your offspring and your flocks, [[11:1|and thrust you out|et exire compellet]] [literally "and shall compel you to go out"] for fear of being slain himself. He did not, however, compel them in such a way that the children of Israel went out against their will; but he compelled them, that is, he pressed and urged them importunately and in haste to go out: which the Hebrews too did gladly. [[11:2|Therefore thou shalt tell all the people|Dices ergo omni plebi]] of the Hebrews, [[11:2|that every man ask of his friend|ut postulet vir ab amico suo]], that is, that the Hebrew men ask of the Egyptians who are friendly to them, [[11:2|and every woman of her neighbour|et mulier a vicina sua]], that is, the Hebrew woman of the Egyptian women living near her, [[11:2|vessels of silver and of gold|vasa argentea et aurea]]; and also [[Ex 12:35|very much raiment|vestem plurimam]], or many garments, as is told in the next chapter. [[11:3|And the Lord will give favour to his people in the sight of the Egyptians|Dabit autem Dominus gratiam populo suo coram Ægyptiis]], that is, He will incline the hearts of the Egyptians to be well disposed towards the Hebrews, to favour them and to lend them vessels and garments. Here the manner of speaking changes from the first person to the third. For whereas the Lord had said to Moses in the first person, [[11:1|Yet one plague more will I bring upon Pharao|Adhuc una plaga tangam Pharaonem]], now there is added in the third person, [[11:3|And the Lord will give favour|Dabit autem Dominus gratiam]]. And so the angel who uttered those words in the first person, speaking as it were in the person of God, spoke these words in the third person, in his own person, of God as of another.

paras.t: Circa hæc quæritur, qualiter quidam Ægyptii erant amici fautoresque Hebræorum. Quocirca loquitur Augustinus : In terra Gessen quidam Ægyptii cohabitaverunt Hebræis, ad quos merito Hebræorum potuerunt illa divina beneficia pervenire, ita ut et Hebræos diligerent, et eis faciliter commodarent quod petebant. Nec tamen Deus judicavit illos Ægyptios, ita alienos fuisse ab injuriis et contritionibus Hebræorum, ut damnum istud non paterentur, qui aliis plagis percussi non erant. In his verbis asserit Augustinus, Ægyptios illos in terra Gessen morantes, non fuisse novem plagis præinductis percussos, ideoque dilexisse Hebræos. Hinc et in Glossa asseritur : Ægyptii qui habitabant in terra Gessen cum Hebræis, novem plagis percussi non erant. Ista tamen non videntur consonare prædictis. Et quidam alii ac Josephus aliter sentiunt. Nec potest negari, quin decima plaga percussi sint, quæ facta est ante Hebræorum egressum. Cur ergo non aliis plagis minoribus? Nihilo minus verisimile est, et satis credibile, quod quidam Hebræi cum quibusdam Ægyptiis quamdam amicitiam habuerunt, et propter præhabita signa multi Ægyptii Hebræis vicini, conceperunt reverentiam et affectionem ad eos. Et tales forsan minus afflicti fuerunt plagis præfatis quam ceteri. Nam et sequenti habetur capitulo, quod innumerabile vulgus Ægyptiorum per signa ista conversum, exivit pariter cum Hebræis. In Scholastica quoque fertur historia : Quidam Ægyptiorum timentes Ægyptum perituram, egressi sunt, ut Cecrops, qui ingressus Græciam, condidit urbem quam vocavit Acten, quæ postea dicta est Athenæ.
paras.en: Here it is asked how some Egyptians were friends and well-wishers of the Hebrews. On this Augustine says: "In the land of Gessen some Egyptians lived together with the Hebrews, and those divine benefits could reach them through the merit of the Hebrews, so that they both loved the Hebrews and readily lent them what they asked. Yet God did not judge those Egyptians to have been so free of the wrongs and oppressions done to the Hebrews that they should not suffer this loss, they who had not been struck by the other plagues." In these words Augustine asserts that those Egyptians dwelling in the land of Gessen had not been struck by the nine plagues that went before, and that therefore they loved the Hebrews. Hence the Gloss too asserts: "The Egyptians who lived in the land of Gessen with the Hebrews had not been struck by the nine plagues." This, however, does not seem to agree with what was said earlier. And certain others, and Josephus, think otherwise. Nor can it be denied that they were struck by the tenth plague, which came before the departure of the Hebrews. Why then not by the other, lesser plagues? Nevertheless it is likely, and credible enough, that certain Hebrews had some friendship with certain Egyptians, and that on account of the signs already given many Egyptians who were neighbours of the Hebrews conceived reverence and affection for them. And such people were perhaps less afflicted by those plagues than the rest. For it is told in the next chapter too that a countless multitude of Egyptians, converted by these signs, went out together with the Hebrews. And in the *Scholastic History* it is related: "Some of the Egyptians, fearing that Egypt would perish, went away, like Cecrops, who came into Greece and founded a city which he called Acte, which was afterwards called Athens."
